name: The twofold argument for Christian belief
plain_explanation: Early Christian apologists argued for their faith in two ways at once: first, that reason alone (without needing the Bible) can establish God, immortality, and free will; second, that the Bible proves much more than that, and its divine origin is shown by fulfilled prophecy, miracles, and the good lives believers as a result.
precise_definition: Origen's apologetic structure (in Against Celsus): (1) 'pure reason, rightly exercised,' suffices to establish essentials of the Christian faith -- God, immortality, free will; (2) Scripture proves these and more, its inspiration evidenced by fulfilled prophecy ('manifestation of the Spirit'), miracles ('power'), and the beneficial effects of Christian belief on believers' lives.
why_it_mattered: Russell identifies this as the standard argumentative structure of Christian philosophy from Origen until the Renaissance, with the 'beneficent effects on believers' argument still used as late as William James.
historical_origin: Articulated by Origen against the pagan critic Celsus.
examples: The appeal to Old Testament prophecy as proof of Christ's coming
The appeal to miracles as continuing evidence of divine power
objections: Some parts (e.g., prophecy-fulfillment arguments) are, in Russell's own view, 'now considered out of date'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Recurs throughout the Christian philosophical tradition Russell surveys in Book Two.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: A tool of religious apologetics used in direct controversy with pagan critics such as Celsus.
